title: Pro Sports Has a Moon-Landing Conspiracy Problem

Pro Sports Has a Moon-Landing Conspiracy Problem
It caused barely a ripple — maybe because most people who heard it couldn’t quite believe it? Last month Drake Maye, the starting quarterback for the New England Patriots, revealed that he’s “a little bit skeptical” about the 1969 moon landing. Skeptical — as in, not entirely sold on that whole one-giant-leap-for-mankind thing.
Mr. Maye made this alarming confession during his weekly segment on Boston’s WEEI-FM, a spot normally given over to empty platitudes and jock-speak, but an intrepid caller asked Mr. Maye if he subscribes to any conspiracy theories — and whew, boy. “Let me try not to get too controversial,” he said. “I don’t know about the moon, you know,” adding, “I’m not really sure 200 percent if we went there or not.”
My first thought on hearing this was: Huh. All these years I’ve been laboring under the impression that the moon landing was among my earliest and most cherished memories, and now it turns out those memories were a sham. According to Mr. Maye — and one of the show’s hosts, who eagerly co-signed Mr. Maye’s skepticism — I need to wake up, along with the 600 million other people who thought they were witnessing history.
Then I had a second thought. If Mr. Maye and I have anything in common, it might be that we’re both reluctant to automatically believe everything we hear. So I allowed myself to wonder if that wasn’t the real Drake Maye on the radio but, rather, some ingenious Maye impersonator. Alas, a quick internet search revealed that the quarterback wasn’t being impersonated. It was all too real.
At which point I pivoted again. In my mind, I began reaching out to Mr. Maye. While rinsing dishes, checking email, I composed a respectful but impassioned letter, and fantasized about FedEx-ing it to Patriots HQ, tucked inside “Of a Fire on the Moon,” Norman Mailer’s deeply felt paean to Apollo 11.
“Dear Mr. Maye: You went to Chapel Hill, right? Fantastic center of higher education! I love that campus. I’ve known several brilliant U.N.C. graduates, so I need to ask: Was the library undergoing some sort of renovation while you were there? Were students prevented from entering that building during your time?”
